title: Memory clinic social work: systematic review of caregiver burden screening, a bad appraisal and an invented claim withdrawn
notes: Adversarial path on a clear systematic review. A fixture search returns seven records, one an undated service evaluation (year null). The appraisal (S13) carries two impossible values: methodQuality 140 for the controlled before-after study, stored null with issue out-of-range, and year true for the language study, which appraisal may not change at all: it is dropped with an issue and the retrieved year 2024 stays (identity is not annotatable; G4). Four claims are recorded, certainty 'low'. The first design reply recommends introducing screening now and rests on claims 'c7' and 'c8', which do not exist (the ledger holds c1 to c4), with a care-home figure no record reports: both ids are dropped with issues, the decision has no supporting claim, and the investigator's acceptance must be refused (G7; S1, S8). The investigator then withdraws the unsupported proposal explicitly. The second design reply proposes the review itself, resting on c1 to c3, with both gates met on the investigator's facts (library request LIB-2026-118 and the second reviewer's agreement), so the accepted action is ready. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59, computed by the generator script: 'ev-' plus the base-36 FNV-1a hash of the normalised DOI (records 1 ev-0ki66sr, 2 ev-1wipjr9, 3 ev-0sah649, 6 ev-0v3su9j), or of titleYearKey(title, year) when there is no DOI (records 4 ev-050srri, 5 ev-1crfqbs, 7 ev-0vy0yf3). Catches: out-of-range scores stored as values, a model changing a retrieved record's year, acceptance of a decision resting on invented claims, and an implementation recommendation dressed as evidence.

inputs.need:
I am the senior social worker in the memory clinic at Ashby Lane Hospital. About 640 people are referred to us each year with suspected dementia, and at most first visits a family member comes too. We know that many of these caregivers are exhausted, but whether we ask about it depends on which clinician they see: two of our five clinicians use a 12-item caregiver burden scale, the others ask informally or not at all, and referral to carer support, respite or counselling is patchy.

Our clinic manager would like all caregivers to be screened for burden at the first visit and again every six months, with referral to support services when the score is high. Before we commit clinician time, I want to do a systematic review of whether routine caregiver burden screening in memory clinics or similar specialist services, followed by referral or support, improves outcomes for caregivers (burden, depression, quality of life) or for the person with dementia (for example, a delayed move to a care home). I suspect that most studies test support programs rather than screening itself, so the review has to be careful about what exactly was compared.

I also want to know whether screening works equally well for caregivers who are spouses, adult children or friends, for men and women, and for caregivers who do not speak English well. A clinic psychologist has agreed to be the second reviewer, and the hospital library can run the searches. We need a focused question, clear eligibility criteria, and a synthesis plan that fits what the studies actually measured.
inputs.constraints: Two reviewers (the investigator and a clinic psychologist) with about 50 hours each before May 2027. The hospital library runs the searches. No translation budget; English and Spanish reports only.

response.title: Routine caregiver burden screening in memory clinics and outcomes for caregivers and people with dementia: a systematic review
response.subtitle: Evidence for a decision on routine screening at first visit and every six months
response.statement: Family caregivers attending the memory clinic are screened for burden inconsistently, and referral to support is patchy. Before committing clinician time to routine screening, the clinic needs to know whether screening followed by referral or support improves caregiver burden, depression or quality of life, or delays care home admission, and whether it works equally for different caregivers. Most studies may test support rather than screening, so the comparison must be defined carefully.

records.title: Routine caregiver burden screening at a memory clinic followed by social work referral: a controlled before-after study
records.authors: Ellison-Adeyemi F, Carvalho-Nyberg J, Obi-Hartley S
records.abstract: One memory clinic introduced routine burden screening of family caregivers at the first visit and every six months, with social work referral for high scores; a second clinic continued usual care. Among 310 caregivers followed for 12 months, burden scores (0 to 48) fell by a mean of 3.1 points in the screening clinic and 0.8 points in the comparison clinic. A positive depression screen was less common at 12 months in the screening clinic (24 against 33 percent). Moves of the person with dementia to a care home did not differ. Clinics differed in staffing and caseload.

records.title: Screening family caregivers of people with dementia: a systematic review of screening tools and their measurement properties
records.abstract: We identified 23 studies evaluating nine caregiver burden screening tools. Most tools correlated moderately with depression and quality of life measures, and short versions of 4 to 12 items performed similarly to longer ones. Cut-off scores for high burden varied between studies and settings. No included study tested whether screening itself, as opposed to the tools' measurement properties, changed caregiver outcomes. Few studies included caregivers who were not spouses or who spoke a language other than the tool's original language.

records.title: Multicomponent support for dementia caregivers identified through specialist services: a randomised trial
records.authors: Kawashima-Doyle T, Afolabi-Strand R, Petersen-Iwu M
records.abstract: We randomised 256 caregivers with high burden scores, identified in three specialist dementia services, to six months of multicomponent support (counselling, skills training and respite planning) or to usual care. Burden scores fell by 4.2 points with support and 1.5 points with usual care at six months. At 24 months, 21 percent of people with dementia in the support group and 27 percent in the usual-care group had moved to a care home, a difference with a wide confidence interval. The trial tested support for screened caregivers, not screening itself.

records.title: Who is missed by caregiver burden screening? Language, relationship and gender in a memory clinic
records.abstract: We examined which of 480 family caregivers attending a memory clinic completed a burden screen. Screening was completed for 86 percent of spouses and 64 percent of adult children, who attended visits less often. Only 41 percent of caregivers with limited English completed the screen, mainly because translated versions were not available. Men reported lower burden scores than women but more often declined referral when their score was high. The authors recommend offering screening outside visits and in the caregiver's language.

records.title: Referral uptake after caregiver screening in specialist dementia services
records.venue: Social Work in Health Care Settings
records.abstract: Across four specialist dementia services, we followed 390 caregivers referred to support after a high burden score. Only 38 percent attended the support service within three months. Uptake was higher when the referring clinician named a contact person and introduced the service on the same day (52 percent) than when a leaflet was given (24 percent). Caregivers who did not attend most often cited lack of time and the difficulty of leaving the person with dementia alone. Referral uptake was not recorded by relationship to the person with dementia.

records.title: Caregiver burden and time to care home admission of people with dementia: a cohort study
records.abstract: We followed 1,140 people with dementia and their family caregivers from diagnosis for up to five years. High caregiver burden at diagnosis was associated with earlier admission of the person with dementia to a care home (hazard ratio 1.46, 95 percent CI 1.21 to 1.76) after adjustment for dementia severity, age and living arrangements. Burden was measured only once, and changes in burden over time were not captured. The association does not show that reducing burden would delay admission, because families under strain may also differ in resources and in their wishes about care.

records.title: Screening and support for family caregivers in memory services: a regional service evaluation
records.abstract: This report describes a regional program in which memory services offered burden screening to family caregivers at diagnosis. Of 1,900 caregivers screened, 12 percent scored in the high burden range and were offered referral. The report describes how the program was organised, staff training and the referral pathways used. Caregiver outcomes were not measured, and the report does not state when the evaluation took place or how caregivers were selected for screening. Staff described the time needed to discuss scores as the main barrier to routine use.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Only one controlled study tested screening itself and found a modest additional fall in burden; a randomised trial shows that support helps caregivers once they are identified. Screening misses adult children and caregivers with limited English, and most referred caregivers never reach support. High burden predicts earlier care home admission, but no study shows that screening delays it. The evidence justifies a review that separates screening from support.
response.gradeRationale: One non-randomised study of screening, indirect randomised evidence on support, and observational equity and uptake data; serious risk of bias and indirectness.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four claims recorded; overall certainty low.

response.reading: Screening can only help through what follows it: a referral that the caregiver takes up, and support that works. The retrieved evidence is strongest for the last link (support for identified caregivers) and weakest for screening itself. Two leaks sit between them: who gets screened (spouses more than adult children, English speakers more than others) and who takes up referral.
